newsitem.title: BURUNDI: 20,000 Burundi refugees return home but need help.
newsitem.headline: 20,000 Burundi refugees return home but need help.

text.p: A total of 20,000 Burundian Hutu refugees have returned home from East Zaire camps but lack clean water or food, the U.N.'s World Food Programme (WFP) said on Friday.

The returnees were discovered at Buganda commune close to the Zairean border in troubled Cibitoke province during an exploratory trip by U.N agencies heavily guarded by Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army.
"We are talking about 20,000 refugees who have come back spontaneously from Zaire," said Jean-Luc Siblot, WFP Burundi representative.

"They have been put into four camps by the authorities but security does not allow them to be fed and they have nothing so they have stolen from local residents. But many do not have blankets or food or medicines so it is absolutely urgent that we do something," he said.
The returnees represent the biggest group to go home since up to a million refugees fled camps in Eastern Zaire when ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels took control from the Zairean army.
Around 140,000 Burundian Hutu refugees fled camps north of Uvira in Eastern Zaire three weeks ago because of the fighting and 70 percent remain unaccounted for.

A total of 20,000 crossed the Rusizi river bordering Burundi and Zaire in the three weeks since the fall of the Uvira camps and 12,000 had been registered at Gatumba camp west of the capital Bujumbura.

East African states imposed sanctions on Burundi after a military coup on July 25 and are still restricting imports of fuel and food for humanitarian purposes despite formally relaxing the embargo last month, Siblot said.

Siblot appealed to East African states to relax sanctions on humanitarian aid, arguing an operation to assist the Cibitoke returnees and refugees still in Zaire from Burundi would be impossible because of the bureaucracy imposed by sanctions.
"It is absolutely imperative that this question of sanctions on food and fuel is resolved because otherwise we will not be able to operate," Siblot said.
Any attempt to mount a cross-border relief operation into Zaire from Burundi for an unknown number of displaced refugeees and Zaireans would be hampered by Burundi's isolation under sanctions.
The call could force East African states including Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda to re-think sanctions on Burundi in the light of a more pressing regional humanitarian crisis.
Siblot said up to 3,000 other returnees, trucked back to Cibitoke's Rugombo commune this week from Gatumba were living in "absolutely terrible" conditions with no access to clean water.

Months of civil war had left water pipes destoyed and refugees were forced to drink from a dirty irrigation channel or from the Rusizi, but the U.N. hoped to begin providing for the returnees next week.
Aid workers expressed grave security concerns about a government plan this week to take Hutu returnees back to their home communes in Cibitoke.
Up to 130 returnees have disappeared, presumed killed by the Burundian army at the border in an operation to separate refugees from suspected Hutu rebels, aid workers and diplomats say.
Around 150,000 people have been killed in three years of civil war in Burundi and Cibitoke province, until now rated a no-go area by aid agencies, has seen the worst of the fighting.
